author: @mrdali67

text:
@vortraz2054  That's the joke.png
Anyway what really impressed me is the degree to which you can see the whole overengineered design process play out like an absolute meme. You can literally see as he's pulling it apart all the contradictory effort going into it on the part of multiple different teams and groups of people with highly different ideas and wildly different priorities. I mean, just the ARGB like lol I'm not knocking it but WHY. Like they took all the effort to do all that for not very spectacular RGB effect, and then proceed to f'ing glue it, so if it ever dies good luck with that. Or the completely senseless way they screwed down the fan cables to make it rigid as possible, only to have a flimsy piece of tape holding it together.

Really, it's a modern work of art in its own right, the artist giving a poignantly biting commentary on the nature of the design process in megacorps.

https://i.pinimg.com/originals/6c/81/2d/6c812d364752418eba3c64a1060d15ce.png

I feel like a LOT of people here can relate to that pic about the project design process

text:
The glue situation is just terrible. A reason for me not to buy this card, even if the drivers weren't complete garbage. I do replace the GPU stock fans after the warranty expires for all my GPU's. 

I had an GTX 660Ti in my living room PC for many years and after the fans have died, i grabbed my solder iron and some noctua 90mm fans. It not only fixed my GPU, but also made it more quiet and cool. This convinced me, that the proprietary fans used by GPU manufacturers are just not that good. I have noctua-modded some other cards - After the warranty expired of course - and it was always worth it. The warranty of my EVGA RTX 2070s will expire next year and i will put three noctua 120mm fans on it with a low noise adaptor.

drivers are already solving most of these issues, and, my friends and i went with the acer bifrost a770 16gb... 5 of us so far... having less trouble then we expected, dxvk solves most issues... well now its not needed so much as its being baked in, but, yeah.... its not bard hardware, its drivers that need matured alot.. as to 3070perf..depending on the game this at times matches the 3070ti, very dependent on drivers but, they are advancing quickly.... from dual 1070 amp extreme push the limit cards to a770+1070amp extreme ptl with the nvidia card being virtually unused... even got my 4 monitors on the arc rather then split between them... so yeah... 

we all were using dxvk on nvidia and amd hardware already so most games just worked like we upgraded our hardware, even with the pre-dxvk-bake-in drivers.. 

for all the crap talking  even GN have changed their view.. i could tell it was drivers when i saw my buddies a380 perf on linux... better then 3050ti 1650ti and even 1660ti for some titles and emulation.., in windows it was pretty bad-horrible without  dxvk though till the 3059 drivers, since then all arc drivers are ALOT better, still not perfect but, no worse then my last time on AMD when the ReLive drivers and later drove alot us legacy users to change to Pascal based cards(1070 in my case)... 

no joke, this is giving me 1070sli perf in 1 card that uses less power then the 2 its replaced for gaming... not really had any issues i couldnt solve with dxvk/vkd3d though... and its so eas to install i laugh when people act like it requires skills... yuou download a file, open it, copy the files you need from the x32 or x64 folder to the games folder and.. wow dxvk is working.. text:
The fans have a steel back-plate that holds them "rigid" to the fan shroud. The sole purpose of the tape is to route the wiring down these back-plates. 
Just about anybody could whip up those PCB designs and have them shipped by the dozens for only a few dollars from China, obviously Intel pays significantly less since they'd order them by the thousands+. 
The acrylic LED frames are also cheap to produce and anybody with a laser cutter or CNC could replicate and build them very quick and pretty cheap while still making a profit. 
The double-sided tape isn't bad, it's just a beauty panel, no harm there. Good double-sided tape is very cheap and even the simplest of humans can apply fresh tape to stick it back down.
Does the average user really repair or modify their GPU? Short of regularly changing out thermal compound.. I assume, with how many customers pay me to service their gear, that most of this is a non-issue for most people, and the performance of the GPU should be the primary concern.

text:
I don't expect them to be perfect. But Intel is NOT new to the PC market, and there are certain items overlooked in this GPU that are a no-brainer to me. Take that double-sided tape - it's probably not going to hold up to heat, and even if it does, heat softens adhesives - I anticipate some complaints of "buzzing" in a few years. The ribbon-thin circuit boards of LEDs is highly-susceptible to heat and flex. The entire design seems overly-complex for a company dipping their toes into the waters of GPU production.

It would make more sense to build more simply, not take a Rube-Goldberg attitude when it comes to design & layout. Simpler designs are typically more robust, and the money saved in the engineering phase could mean a lower price point - making them an even stronger contender in the market.

I do want them to succeed in this endeavor, as I believe competition not only drives innovation, but encourages companies to build a better product at a better price point. I'm just concerned that they're trying to do too much too soon, and might end up squandering the chance to become a serious competitor in a market that needs that competition.

text:
Well, I have mixed feelings because on one side I can see a deep attention to details like those led strips and PCBs. A modern type of cooler - many manufacturers are using only heat pipes. On the other side I see some cables sticked with tape and some daughter boards like it was invented just a few days before release date and added in the last moment.

I don't mind them using double side tape for that backplate cover. A screwless design LOOK(only) has something that I can understand manufacturers might look for. It's like bolts covers for aluminium wheels in cars. You know they are there, but are covered for that fine, elegant look.

About replacing the GPU fans - did anyone of you did that in practise? I have had some GPUs for a long time and none of them had a fan failure. I did once a Frankenstein mod to replace 80mm high speed fan to a bigger, lower RPM one that was simply quieter. This are the kind of mods I would do to an older GPU. Looking for a replacement untypical fans for old GPU is just too expensive. Grab a pair of dexent quality 120mm and zip tie it to a heatsink. It is very possible that you will get similar performance to stock fans with less noise except 70-100% fan speed on stock fans, but who uses that? Anything above 2000rpms on a stock fans is quite loud.

text:
Seeing this complexity, I'm glad we have a 5 year warranty mandated by law in Norway.
Any product that is meant to last longer than 2 years, gets a 5 year warranty at minimum, or as high as the manufacturer states.
That includes video cards, CPUs, hard drives, mobile phones, cars, etc.
Typical cheaper items like phone covers, items that are worn down by design gets a 2 year minimum warranty, or as high as the manufacturer states. 
And the retailers that sell these items rarely ever argue about it. I had a 3 year old GTX 1080 where the fan started having issues, I RMA'ed it, and received an RTX 2070 instead. 
One would think that it would result in higher prices, but it really doesn't. The average electronics prices are about the typical European level. Which is USA price + VAT about 25%.

text:
I actually think this card is pretty well designed. It managed to pull a very refined look without relying on glue, plastic clips, or (almost any) other attachment methods that have limited lifespan.

Yes, the screw count is huge, but for most servicing a few screws gets you there, most repairs can be done with large component swaps (I/E fan shroud assembly), and everything except those LED ring diffusers looks to be very easily replaced without risking permanent damage to any other part.

Also your argument of argument of "because the drivers are bad the product is bad and the money is wasted in product design" is pretty a bad take. Not everything can be solved by throwing more money at the problem, and putting less effort, care and quality in the manufacturing and product design would not make it any better.
Particularly when hardware is immutable whilst software can be fixed in the future.

text:
I mean we need to recognise these are $300 low end cards, so despite it being "best Intel can offer", they really compare in build quality to 3050 or Radeon 6500. I would not expect to find high quality alloys or magnets in the design, just plastic frame. That said using glue and double-sided take is still very poor design, there is no way around it. However, what I have noticed and what is even more questionable is why the card is whole inch longer than it needs to be. Clearly PCB ends whole inch short, there is no pass thought design, even radiator doesn't extend there. So it is just literally empty space for dust to accumulate. I guess they maybe did it for "symmetry" but still it looks kind of odd. As well intel knows that they will have to discount these to like $150 to sell or just send them to landfill 2 years later, so I think not investing too much into quality does make sense.

That said just looks wise I generally like it, it looks solid... what I hate however is nvidia 4090 - if you have to make radiator that big, then you should have gone AiO (same applies to 3090 and 3090Ti), it should not be air cooled card and 3+ slot design is just silly. Overall, the looks is ok and I generally liked 3080/3080Ti looks, it is not childish, but truth to be told it is overcomplicated for no reason and it is ineffective design for cooling. 3080Ti in particular was real jet engine in the PC - hot and loud... and you need to manually set fan cure quite aggressively if you don't want it to burn down your PC and home. So as far as intel is considered I think their design is acceptable, but lazy and cheap (somewhat justifiable in low end product) and as far as Nvidia goes - they are stupid, just go AiO if you can fit the card in 2 slots.

text:
Has anybody considered the fact that glue's adhesive properties degrade with both temperature and time? Add to that some air pressure (from the fans), and... people should definitely watch out for that thin back plate flying off the card... and, since it's made of (conductive) aluminum, maybe even causing a shortcut or two on the motherboard?

This problem should become obvious with a couple of years in use, with Intel probably hoping not before the warranty expires. After that... they (obviously) truly, honestly don't care.

Even as a showcase product, never intended to actually be sold to end users, this is a terrible, terrible display of incompetence on every possible level. All the way from the top managers making impossible demands down to lowly engineers turning those impossible demands into genuinely bad products.

This is, for all intents and purposes, Chinese level of product "quality"... and I've got some cheap* aluminum Chinese knives to sell to Intel, which are (if you can believe it, I couldn't even though I held them in my hands) even thinner than that back plate.

* Excellent price-to-performance!

text:
@h3ftymouse , all valid points. I wrote my comment before I saw GN's performance review of the card and checked pricing. Or rather, anticipated pricing, since the GPU isn't yet available as I write this. As far as worries about repair are concerned, I was mainly concerned about one or both fans failing after a few years of use. The fans in this card don't appear to be all that great, and if the street pricing ends up being around the anticipated MSRP of $350, i wouldn't be too happy about having to either replace the card due to fan failure after 2-3 years or figure out how to replace the fans.

I should add that while I do build desktop PCs for clients, I don't build a lot of gaming rigs. I'm mostly interested in reliable GPUs for clients who need them for graphic design and video editing applications, and most of the GPUs I consider for them fall in the performance range of this one. text:
In case anyone was curious, the fabric tape they're using is high-temp wiring loom tape. It's fantastic stuff because it bonds well to paint, plastic, nylon, and even smooth-finish silicone as it is meant to wrap wiring looms in automotive production. It is also very thin and doesn't readily lose its adhesion like Kapton tape sometimes does over time. It makes sense that they'd use a product seemingly purpose-built for wire management to manage their wires.

 Honestly, I'd rather have all of the little auxiliary PCBs for LED management if it means they can use fewer, easier to manage cables instead of really going out of their way to create a rat's nest of cables inside the housing. As long as the plugs that go into the connectors are obvious, labeled, or don't need to be removed to service the card then I'm largely fine with their implementation, as it makes the card relatively tidy for the amount of LEDs they're using. I'd much rather them have an absolute stunner of a card that is slightly less convenient to disassemble than make something that looks boring or trashy as their "Limited Edition" flagship product. But it's still a game of qualifiers. If the card didn't look so good and wasn't priced so competitive to its performance level, then I'd be less forgiving of these minor annoyances. 

Also, a pair of forceps is a fantastic tool for pulling connectors from their sockets, particularly if you can get right-angle ones.

All in all, an annoying GPU to work on, but at least they're trying to use quality components so you hopefully won't need to. At the very least, if your card doesn't arrive DoA then it should last until the next model gets released, assuming Intel doesn't follow through on axing the whole project.

Apart from less-than-100-screws screwless design marketing claim, there's serious heat management flaw on that particular graphic card. In 18:06 (PCB) and 19:12 (thermal pads on heatsink) we could clearly see pads that had contact only with lower half of top 4 memory chips. I wonder if they were so absorbed with all that LED circus around to think about such non-essential detail as overheating memory.
The rest – glue, tape, wiring braided through holes in chassis looks like last night stunt before trade show. That way maybe will do for movie prop but not for something to be manufactured in reasonable quantities. There's no way to automate assembly of this contraption.

text:
23:47 These custom thin PCBs are even worse than they look, because PCBs are cut from big flat sheets and those layouts (especially the long U-shaped one) don't meaningfully nest/tile to panelize efficiently. By comparison, things like straight thin boards or L shapes can be tiled closely on a larger sheet to make efficient use of the stock material. 

That means every one of those they produce involves throwing out or recycling a huge amount of PCB stock material to get the shapes in question unless they happen to have other parts of the design (or similar designs) that can nest inside these during production. The main board itself can't, because it's an entirely different process with many more PCB layers than these flimsy little LED strips. Absolutely insane design on these cards; Intel could probably shave at least $50 off the cost just by redesigning these cards for actual manufacturability.

This design is similar to many laptops but more specifically there were these old Dells from, I believe, the early to mid 2000's that once you took the top half (palmrest keyboard assembly) off you were presented with a frame of sorts that all kinds of wires and things were interwoven through. Up on reassembly, remembering which part of the frame certain wires and even components, i.e. USB board or NIC, went over or under was impossible to remember. It's been a while since dealing with that so exact details have been forgotten but it was a nightmare of a design, I know that. Watching this tear down brought back those nightmares. Thanks Steve! 😉

text:
Its actually easy to assemble (from sub-assemblies) and not designed for servicability. That has been the mantra of most manufacturers for over twenty years. Manufacturers pay for the manufacturing cost (transformation costs). They, and Engineering have no mandate to make it easy to repair. It must last for the duration of the warranty period (with minimal statistical variance) and nothing else. Service is not a profit center.
That can be argued as valid for a fairly low cost consumable whose marketability period is finite. (There will be a new series with most of the sold units still functioning.) That does not make sense for say a $130,000 EV. In the latter case the cost is so high (and financing so long) that it must last for at least the duration of the financing.  Thereafter it becomes a battle of the curves for cost of repair/maintenance vs just buying entirely new.

text:
"We wanted the light box to highlight the problems with the card"

And in a single statement it highlights my love / hate relationship with Gamers Nexus.  I love what GN does.  I love that they call out BS in the industry.  I love that they call out marketing BS.  But some (NOTE SOME NOT ALL.) of what is brought up feels like theatrics to entice people to watch their videos to find out what Steve is going to complain about this time.
A few things of note.
-You put the double sided tape face down....and complain about it with a grumble.....do you make a peanut butter sandwich, and then before going to the other slice you place it face down? 
-Complaining about double sided tape when a roll costs $3 at Target.  I have 3, 3M rolls in my house for random use.  This is a pedantic complaint. Would it be better if it was screws?  Yes.  Is it that big of a deal for anyone who is taking apart a GPU to replace parts that cost far more then double sided tape?  No because its the cover.  If you had used a heat gun when you realized there was tape there that would have come right off.  (And yes I'm aware not everyone has a heat gun, but most do have a hair dryer.) But again theatrics.  It makes for good viewer retention when you can hem and haw about something.  
-Complaining about LED cables....really?
-"I would be impressed with this if....ahhh....."    Impressive a complimenting complaint.  

That said.  A lot of shots are well deserved.  The short interconnect to the daughterboard screams either they added that later in the design and didn't plan for that to begin with, or simply created a kludge were designs were an afterthought as just ship it mentality was more important. (We saw this kind crap on Dell laptops in the early 2K's.) The 15 billion screw types, the custom solution with the LED's,  speak to this being more of a kludge than anything else.  Manufacturing date was what?  Feb / 2022?  That means manufacturing probably started in 2021.  And we are launching now?  Why now?  Purely drivers?  Or multiple revisions of something in design in assembly?

The thing is my complaint doesn't have anything to do with fanboiing for Intel.  It was just the final instance where eye roll after eye roll over the last year finally resulted in them rolling out of the sockets this time around.  I'm not expecting glowing reviews of anything.  It would be rare to find flawless products.  Finding and expositing those flaws is fine, hell expected even.  But a cover plate held in place by tape, or freaking about any tape isn't a OMG thing to get bent out of shape over.  The complex nature of disassembly IS.  This is right up there with some Alienware laptops I had to repair in my hellish stint doing warranty work.  I appreciated everything GN does for the community but the perceived theatrics

It not having screws would be a disaster, and you're well aware of that, given your previous stance on serviceability.  Obviously the screwless shroud was a trade off between aesthetics and ease of serviceability, and I'm with you that it's not great, but come on, it's not like intel said "entirely screwless" and if they had, it would have been terrible, so why pretend that's what they said 8 different times in the video?  Looking at my 3080, there are tons of visible screws, I don't mind, but it's a totally different aesthetic and obviously that is what they are advertising.

Look, you made great points about serviceability and right to repair, but the hyperbole and apparent confirmation bias make it really hard to trust that you'll accurately speak to things they've done well or gotten right, or that you're providing a generally unbiased opinion (even if it happens to be negative).

text:
To be fair, first versions of product lines that are new to a vendor are likely to be exactly as you found: difficult, hard to manufacture, etc.  Goal is to get the product out as fast as possible (obviously, it's the same with the drivers).

Surely Intel is undergoing a v2.0 redesign, and though I have essentially zero manufacturing experience, there are obvious opportunities for improvement.

For starters, a fan assembly with unified bracket (from Cooler Master, possibly) could be created with several less screws and way less tape; one end slides under a retaining clip on the far end, screw holds it in place on the other end. Probably easier cable management too.

That big round single-layer circular PCB around the fans (providing the LEDs) likewise could easily use simple snap-in clips and no screws.

Many of the cable harnesses could be consolidated to make assembly (and disassembly) easier.

This will get fixed, but hopefully not before the fix the damn drivers!

author: @infernaldaedra

text:
@infernaldaedra  that usually has more to do with the material the fastener is made from and how it's been heat treated, as long as your driver is decent quality (machined within whatever specification/ tolerance) and not worn out or being used incorrectly. On electronics with small fasteners torx is better in my opinion, but larger torx bolts such as in automotive applications get rust and dirt in them and it becomes difficult to insert the proper tool

fun fact: there is a Japanese variant of what's usually called a "philips" type screw drive. usually identified by a single dot between two of the lobes. if you've ever thought a philips screwdriver just didn't quite fit right, especially working on something Japenese, you might be using the wrong tool. Specification is called JIS B4633 if anybody is interested in further reading

text: Love your work and I value your opinions in my purchases. I design PCB's for automotive use for a living. I can add a little insight to one part of this. That LED ring PCB isn't actually the worst idea from a design standpoint. It's extremally simple and you'd be surprised how cheap it would be to manufacture especially in bulk. text:
Yeah the fan circles 24:18 and led shroud pcb 24:00 fit neatly inside one another and the space inside each circle is enough for the ARC led pcb 13:11 and that other LED pcb 11:54 are all probably made in one piece so it isn't as wasteful as people would expect. 
The use of threaded inserts where "wood" screws into hollow plastic posts would've sufficed means this was designed by someone used to low volume production though.

text:
Heyoh, i build systems for automotive. And i really liked these LED-PCB's and they are really cheap if you consider all functions they do.
What i don't like at all are those extra power PCB. You have a connector from a PCB, to a PCB to get to a PCB in on single unit ... just why. It's like 3-5 bucks and a punch of possible failures for nothing.
Also casing any PCB in plastic was never a good idea ever ...but we tend to do it all the time ...

The build of this thing reminds me of AvE's excellent Juicero teardown. No expense spared, engineers getting to go wild with a nigh-unlimited budget, beautiful parts (those thin PCBs for lighting! the light+fan daughterboard, packed with smarts and connectors!) no real consideration for servicing, built to hide everything that reveals it was a normal piece of hardware held together with normal screws. 

At least it looks like it would make a handsome card when freed from its plastic prison and having the skinny fans replaced by two big Noctuas. Not that it'd need it, but it's what I thought immediately from that monolithic fin stack.

text: Nobody likes crazy, elaborate designs more than smartphone engineers. They will use half a dozen flat-flex ribbon cables to shave half a millimeter off of the packaging size of the components compared to just building a larger PCB. They also love auxiliary PCBs more than any other industry, because it lets them move things around to wherever they have space left for it. And that's before we get to the last couple of generations of phones where the modern "sandwich PCB" has come into common use, where they basically use soldered connectors to bind two layers of PCB together with basically no gap between them so they can squeeze as much components into the most compact space possible. We should just be glad that Intel didn't hire smartphone PCB engineers for their GPUs. We should also probably be grateful that laptops haven't started to use those designs, because then they would be even less repairable.

text:
Hi GN! I'm a PCB designer and wanted to make a small comment/correction.

At around 24:54 here, when bending the small fan LED circular PCB, you said it's "basically a one-layer PCB". You have made similar statements in the past, another particular example was about a motherboard. I believe you said one of the EVGA motherboards was very thick because it was a 10-layer PCB.

Generally speaking, PCB layer count and thickness don't correlate with one another. PCB thickness is affected primarily by the thickness of dielectrics BETWEEN those layers. These dielectrics can be anywhere from ~0.1mm to multi-millimeter ones, and those are just the commonly available ones, while the average copper layer is 35um (0.035mm).

Layer count effectively only changes the minimum possible (or practical) thickness, due to the thinnest available dielectrics. In reality, the PCB thickness is usually designed to fit the mechanical constraints of the housing. For example, most PCB fabs default to 1.6mm boards regardless of your layer count, unless you specify a custom stackup.

Funnily enough, I will say that in this case, you were possibly spot on. This is one of the situations where it's possible they were trying to keep the thickness as low as possible (within reasonable manufacturing costs).

text:
Think of it this way, I have 2 holes in my sub assembly, if I use the same screw I can have worker A put screw in holes 1 and 2, no extra transfer of the assembly, and one worker needed. 2 different screws, worker A puts theirs in hole 1, passes the subassembly to worker 2 at the next bench who puts theirs in hole 2. This takes 2 workers and a little longer as there is this transfer of the subassembly in the middle.

Now sure, worker 1 can start on their next put screw in hole on the next assembly on the line. But I could also just have 2 workers doing 2 of the same screw to parallize, the extra assembly transfer time is still removed.
author: @EwanMarshall

text: And this is all before I add the chances of workers making a mistake and putting the wrong screw in the wrong hole because they are tired or whatever.
author: @EwanMarshall

text:
@EwanMarshall not if the assembly comes with different screws already installed.

They aren't contracting out the subassemblies to keep track of screws. They're doing it because the hard to automate labor is cheap in Vietnam or wherever. They build the assembly to a point that it's easy to automate and then that assembly is on the build-to BOM that the final integrator uses, probably in the USA do they can stamp "assembled in USA" on it somewhere.

It was either build to spec with an ICD or its Intel's design and the sub asked if they could sub in whatever screws they wanted and Intel didn't care.

It's possible this is just messy Intel design but I kind of doubt they had much to do with the details beyond the high level architecture, at least with respect to its physical implementation.

text:

For screws multiple workbenches is enough, all the contracting you are bringing up does is put a bigger gap between the workbenches.

Yes, there are physical limitations, this is part of optimizing for mass production efficiencies. Sometimes using a different screw is unavoidable, here it is so many different screws in the same part it is surprising.

text:
@Junya01  If you are going with potentially the Rx6600, the next upgrade really should double the performance. Otherwise you are not going to be happy. I don't know anyone, other than bleeding edge enthusiasts, who is actually happy to pay for less than a 50% improvement. For guys like that, power to them I understand the draw, it's just not my thing. Going from an A770 to an RX6600 or vise versa is a side step, really the next step from either of those is a 3070ti or 6800xt, minimum. If you wait several years, the 3080ti may be in the price range. Honestly, the Rx6600 is going to be fine for several years more. AAA games may not be so friendly, but there are hundreds of games that the Rx6600 will play well at 1080p. Which is not 1440p or 4k, but thats really stepping into 3070/3080 or Rx6800/6900 territory.

If you are willing to wait a bit, the 6700 or 6700xt is going to be around 40% more performance average for about 50-75% more cost. Or the 6600xt is a fine competitor with only a marginal difference from the 6700xt while being just a bit cheaper.

text:
@razorblade7108   Right, it's even worse than worthless. Thank you Papa Intel! I feel like GPU manufacturers have been like "let's throw a backplate on it for no reason" for several years now. There are even been GPUs with pointless plastic backplates.

I have more respect for a minimally designed GPU made to reduce costs, than a card with a ton of bloat with no thought put into the big picture. There are other ways to add value other than making a product look flashy. EVGA gained its reputation thanks to its stellar warranties. Leaning towards right to repair by providing board schematics is another way to add perceived value. I feel like that's the only thing Intel can put on the table at this point — other than better GPU drivers.
